youtube.title: Perseus Black Hole: One Note Every 10 Million Years
youtube.description:
Imagine hearing a sound that only happens once every ten million years. NASA scientists took the Perseus galaxy cluster's black hole hum and scaled it up quadrillions of times just for your ears. 

Deep in the Perseus galaxy cluster, a supermassive black hole pumps out sound ripples stretching 300,000 light-years (roughly 1.8 quadrillion miles) wide. While human ears hear 20 to 20,000 vibrations per second, this cosmic note vibrates fifty-seven octaves below middle C.

Sources: NASA Chandra X-ray Observatory - Sounds of the Perseus Galaxy Cluster Black Hole; ESA - Hubble & Chandra Observations of NGC 1275
youtube.pinned_comment: If you could hear this note without scaling it up, would it sound like silence or an absolute hum? 🤔

instagram.caption:
A single vibration every 10 million years. NASA scaled the Perseus black hole's hum quadrillions of times so we could actually hear it. 

How low does your voice go compared to fifty-seven octaves below middle C?

sources: NASA Chandra X-ray Observatory - Sounds of the Perseus Galaxy Cluster Black Hole
ESA - Hubble & Chandra Observations of NGC 1275

fact_checks.claim: This cosmic sound wave vibrates just once every ten million years.
fact_checks.working: NASA/Chandra: the Perseus cluster black hole (NGC 1275) pressure wave has a period of about 10 million years, i.e. frequency ~3.17e-15 Hz. Correct.

fact_checks.claim: Deep in the Perseus galaxy cluster, a supermassive black hole is constantly humming into surrounding gas.
fact_checks.working: Chandra observations show the SMBH in NGC 1275 drives ripples in the surrounding hot X-ray gas. 'Constantly' is acceptable for a sustained, ongoing process over ~10^8 yr, though the wave period itself is 10^7 yr. No numeric error.

fact_checks.claim: It pumps out sound ripples stretching three hundred thousand light-years, roughly 1.8 trillion miles (2.8 trillion km) wide.
fact_checks.working: 1 light-year = 9.4607e12 km = 5.8786e12 miles. 300,000 ly = 300,000 x 9.4607e12 = 2.838e18 km = 2.8 quadrillion km, NOT 2.8 trillion km. In miles: 300,000 x 5.8786e12 = 1.764e18 miles = 1.8 quadrillion miles, NOT 1.8 trillion miles. The script was off by a factor of 1,000,000. Also, the Chandra ripples are typically described as spanning ~300,000 ly across the cluster gas; 'wide' (diameter) is acceptable for the wavefront extent. Fixed to '1.8 quadrillion miles (2.8 quadrillion km)'.

fact_checks.claim: Human ears can only hear sound vibrating between twenty and twenty thousand times per second.
fact_checks.working: Standard human audible range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 to 20,000 cycles per second). Correct.

fact_checks.claim: But this cosmic sound wave vibrates just once every ten million years, fifty-seven octaves below middle C.
fact_checks.working: Period 10^7 yr = 3.156e14 s, frequency = 1/3.156e14 = 3.17e-15 Hz. Middle C (C4) = 261.63 Hz. Octaves = log2(261.63 / 3.17e-15) = log2(8.25e16) = 56.2. NASA/Chandra commonly quote '57 octaves below middle C' (using B-flat or a slightly different reference). Within rounding, 'fifty-seven octaves' matches the official NASA figure. OK.

fact_checks.claim: To make human ears hear it, NASA scientists had to scale the pitch up quadrillions of times.
fact_checks.working: To bring 3.17e-15 Hz into the audible range (~20-20,000 Hz), the scale factor is ~6.3e15 to 6.3e18, i.e. quadrillions (10^15) to quintillions (10^18). 'Quadrillions of times' is a reasonable lower-bound description of the sonification scaling. OK.

fact_checks.claim: If a piano keyboard stretched from Earth to the moon, this note still would not fit on it.
fact_checks.working: Earth-Moon distance = 384,400 km. A piano key is ~2.3 cm wide; 88 keys span ~1.4 m. Even a keyboard with keys 2.3 cm wide stretched 384,400 km would hold ~1.67e10 keys, i.e. ~1.67e10 semitones = ~1.39e9 octaves. The note is only 57 octaves below middle C, so it WOULD easily fit on such a keyboard. The claim is false. Rewritten to a verifiable comparison: the note's wavelength is ~9.5e22 km (~10 billion light-years), far larger than the Earth-Moon distance, so the wave itself would not fit between Earth and the Moon.

fact_checks.claim: A supermassive black hole hums that sound wave once every ten million years.
fact_checks.working: Same as scene 1: period ~10^7 yr. Correct. Note: the black hole itself is not 'humming' audibly; it drives pressure waves in the surrounding gas. The script's framing is consistent with NASA's sonification description.

fact_checks.claim: YouTube description: 'The note sits 57 octaves below middle C, with a period of ten million years.'
fact_checks.working: Matches NASA/Chandra figures. OK.

fact_checks.claim: Instagram caption: 'A supermassive black hole plays a note 57 octaves below middle C.'
fact_checks.working: Matches NASA/Chandra figures. OK.

fact_checks.claim: compare: Milky Way Galaxy 100,000 ly vs Perseus Sound Wavefront 300,000 ly
fact_checks.working: Milky Way diameter ~100,000 ly (commonly cited 100,000-120,000 ly). Perseus ripple extent ~300,000 ly. Same unit (light-years), correct ratio 3:1. OK.
